children: Beijing imposed sweeping exit restrictions on Chinese citizens on Tuesday along with new rules for foreigners entering China, tightening scrutiny of individuals seen as endangering national security, including by violating technology export restrictions.

The measures allow the government to stop Chinese citizens from leaving the country for months or years if they engage in "criminal activities abroad" that threaten national interests or violate export controls that could harm "industrial and technology security."

The restrictions are the latest sign of Chinese leader Xi Jinping's focus on national security and Beijing's heightened attention to curbing the flow of talent and know-how in areas such as artificial intelligence, amid an all-out tech race with Washington.
The rules, which were announced in July by China's State Council, include stepped-up oversight of the movement overseas of Chinese officials and military personnel.
For foreign visitors, the new rules call for punishing those who provide false information in visa applications. They also threaten to deny visas to foreigners on several sanctions lists.

The rules take effect as Beijing has beefed up its export control regime-including on items like rare-earth minerals-and enacted a network of laws to prevent individuals and businesses from complying with foreign sanctions.
Officials have also limited outbound investment and sought to stem the flow of money overseas from the corporate sector and wealthy class in recent months.
The new rules mark the first time that China has explicitly linked violation of export controls with exit restrictions, said Ting Peng, a partner at BZW Law Firm based in Shenzhen.
She added that the rules allow officials to block foreigners from entering the country who are included on several Chinese lists aimed at countering foreign sanctions.

The tech industry has already been affected by exit restrictions in recent months. Beijing told two co-founders of AI firm Manus not to leave China this spring, after Meta Platforms said it would buy the startup in December. Beijing forced Manus to unwind the deal on national security grounds.

The new regulations ensure the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens traveling abroad, as well as national sovereignty and security, government officials said when they were unveiled in July.

Private agencies that handle certain immigration applications by public officials or military personnel in China are now required to report unlawful cases to authorities. That will have a chilling effect on businesses serving customers working in sensitive sectors including tech industries and the government, said an immigration expert in China.
"They will have to be very cautious about their clients," the expert added.
The rules could increase concern among foreigners about travel to China, though the country is experiencing a tourism boom thanks to expanding visa-free entry policies.

Providing false statements when applying for a Chinese visa, or illegally entering or leaving the country, can now mean foreigners are denied entry to China for up to five years. Previously, there was no fixed time limit for visa denial, though the government had the power to block entry, said BZW Law Firm's Peng.
International businesses sending employees to China will also take note, said Chris Carr, a professor at California Polytechnic State University who has studied exit bans in China.
"The overarching lesson for the foreign business community is proceed cautiously and be smart about how you do business within China and who you do it with," he said.
